clue.text: Party manager's plea to manage expectations?

definitions.text: Party manager's plea to manage expectations?

blocks.note: surface reading: an anxious party organiser begging guests to behave
setter's reading: the host's printed request to reply, so they know how many will come

explanation.walkthrough: 'Manage expectations' sounds like office jargon about lowering hopes; here it means literally knowing how many guests to expect. The answer is the French initials printed on invitations.
explanation.definitionFit: The initials ask invited guests to reply, letting a host plan numbers for food and seating.

clue.text: Mawkish, conniving American husband's boring

indicators.note: to bore is to drill into something, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: a conniving person is sly
US is the standard abbreviation for American
H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: A sentimental, scheming American husband turns out to be a crashing bore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring' reads as dull, but it means drilling into: the American and husband go inside the word for conniving.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe excessively sentimental writing or films, gushing with sugary emotion.

clue.text: Harry owes cash for present

indicators.note: to harry is to harass or worry, so the letters are pushed about into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone called Harry owes money, and is short of cash to buy a gift.
explanation.walkthrough: Harry looks like a person's name, but it is a verb meaning to harass, and present is a verb, not a gift.
explanation.definitionFit: To present something is to display it to advantage, which is exactly what you do when you show it off prominently.

clue.text: Fish and wedges hospital binned

indicators.note: something binned is thrown away, so a letter is discarded

blocks.note: wedges are a style of shoe heel
H is the abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs

explanation.surface: A fish-and-chip-shop order: fish and potato wedges, with the hospital food thrown out.
explanation.walkthrough: Wedges suggests potato chips beside the fish, but here they are shoes with wedge heels.
explanation.definitionFit: These long snake-like creatures are a kind of fish, eaten jellied in London.

clue.text: Regularly suss out band together, as is the custom

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so only every other letter is kept

blocks.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters
to ally is to band together

explanation.surface: Checking out a group of people who customarily unite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' looks like part of the definition, meaning habitually, but it picks alternate letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done as is the custom happens normally or habitually, as a matter of routine.

clue.text: Motor slick lad in drainpipes gave the once-over

blocks.note: an Audi is a make of car, a motor in British slang
a Teddy boy was a 1950s British youth with slicked hair and drainpipe trousers

explanation.surface: A slick young man in tight trousers checks out a car.
explanation.walkthrough: Drainpipes are narrow trousers, not plumbing: the slick lad wearing them is a Ted, short for Teddy boy, a 1950s British youth fashion.
explanation.definitionFit: To audit accounts is to inspect them closely, an official examination or inspection.

clue.text: Put down answer in red biro?

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another, here between two neighbours

blocks.note: Che Guevara, the famous revolutionary, is a crossword 'red'
A is the abbreviation for answer
a Biro is a ballpoint pen

explanation.surface: A teacher writing the answer down in red ink.
explanation.walkthrough: Red is a communist, Che Guevara; biro is the British brand name for a ballpoint.
explanation.definitionFit: To put someone down is to belittle them, lowering their worth or dignity.

clue.text: After advance, laconic wit sent up book

indicators.note: laconic means using very few words, so the word is cut to a single letter
in a down clue, sending up turns the letters to read from bottom to top
after places one piece following the other in order

blocks.note: the opening letter
salt means wit, as in Attic salt

explanation.surface: After a pay advance, a dry joker mocks a book.
explanation.walkthrough: Salt is an old word for sharp wit; read upward it follows the clipped first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An atlas is a bound volume of maps, so a kind of book.

clue.text: Newspaper page dealt with after rejecting first piece of copy

indicators.note: to reject is to throw out, so a letter is removed
the first piece of a word is its opening letter

blocks.note: to cope is to deal with something
its opening letter

explanation.surface: An editor handles a newspaper page after spiking the first bit of copy.
explanation.walkthrough: The page sits opposite the editorial and carries outside opinion columns.
explanation.definitionFit: Short for opposite editorial, it is the newspaper section printing signed opinion pieces.

clue.text: District with everyone beginning to steal tyre parts

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter

blocks.note: a side of town is a district of it
W is the abbreviation for with
all means everyone
its opening letter

explanation.surface: A whole neighbourhood starts stealing tyres for parts.
explanation.walkthrough: Side here is a district, as in the East Side of a city.
explanation.definitionFit: The sidewalls are the flexible rubber flanks of a tyre between tread and rim.

clue.text: Devious new clue following edit

indicators.note: something new is made afresh, so the letters are rebuilt in fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written
F is the abbreviation for following, as in page references
taken as written

explanation.surface: A setter rewrites a clue into something more devious after editing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Following' is not a sequence word here but F, the abbreviation used in page references like p. 5f.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe someone who misleads or tricks others through dishonest cunning.

clue.text: Couple swapping, pale and innocent

indicators.note: a pair of neighbours trading places is the same as reading those two the other way

blocks.note: a pasty face is pale and unhealthy-looking

explanation.surface: A wife-swapping couple, pallid and supposedly blameless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Couple swapping' sounds racy, but it just means two adjacent letters, S and T, trade places.
explanation.definitionFit: An innocent, as a noun, is a naive person easily taken in, a dupe or sucker.

clue.text: Long ago in Greece, I thought mountain turning closed

definitions.text: Long ago in Greece, I thought

indicators.note: turning round sends the letters back the way they came

blocks.note: an alp is a mountain
a door that is to is shut

explanation.surface: An ancient Greek recalls a mountain path being closed.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition speaks in the answer's own voice: a thinker of ancient Greece. 'Closed' gives TO, as in pushing a door to.
explanation.definitionFit: The Athenian philosopher lived in classical Greece and is history's archetypal thinker, so he could say this of himself.

clue.text: One stylishly elegant: country's principal girl at welcoming clubs

indicators.note: principal means chief or first, so only the opening letter is taken
to welcome is to take someone in, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: its opening letter
a lass is a girl
taken as written
C is the abbreviation for clubs in card games

explanation.surface: A country's leading lady greets golf clubs with elegance.
explanation.walkthrough: The principal girl is a pantomime role, but here 'principal' just takes the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A class act is a person of real quality and polish, admired for poise and refinement.

clue.text: Smart girl sent to Coventry, then central Merseyside

indicators.note: central means at the very middle, so only the middle letters are kept

blocks.note: to send someone to Coventry is a British idiom for ignoring them, or cutting them
the fifth and sixth of its ten letters

explanation.surface: A clever girl is shunned in Coventry, then moves to Liverpool's county.
explanation.walkthrough: Coventry and Merseyside both suggest a journey across England; sending someone to Coventry means refusing to speak to them. Merseyside is the county around Liverpool.
explanation.definitionFit: A cutey is an attractive young woman, and smart can mean good-looking or stylishly dressed.

clue.text: Yankee tough leaving hotel garden

indicators.note: when something leaves it is gone, so a letter is taken away

blocks.note: Yankee is Y in the NATO alphabet
hard means tough
Hotel is H in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: An American heavy walks out of a hotel into its garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yankee tough' reads as an American thug, but it splits into a letter and an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Americans call the plot behind a house the yard, where Britons would say back garden.

clue.text: Continuum of taxonomic lineage to some extent

indicators.note: to some extent means partly, so only part of the words is used

blocks.note: the end of the first word runs into the start of the second

explanation.surface: A biologist's remark about the gradual spread of a family tree.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface fits the answer neatly, since the word is a biology term for gradual variation within a species.
explanation.definitionFit: A cline is a graded series or gradient of character variation across a population's range.

clue.text: Found cups minute with a cafe treat

indicators.note: to cup is to hold in curved hands, so one piece is enclosed by another

blocks.note: to found something is to create it
M is the abbreviation for minute
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone discovers tiny cups at a café serving a treat.
explanation.walkthrough: Found looks like the past tense of find, but it means establish; cups is a verb, and minute is the abbreviation, not tiny.
explanation.definitionFit: A cream tea is an English afternoon snack of scones with clotted cream, jam and a pot of tea.

clue.text: Opposed to tips for Asian tandoori

indicators.note: tips are the ends, so only the outermost letters of each word are kept

blocks.note: its first and last letters
its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Someone dislikes giving tips at an Indian restaurant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tips' suggests gratuities for the waiter, but they are the end letters of each word.
explanation.definitionFit: Anti is a preposition meaning against, so it can stand for opposed to.

clue.text: As a blaze gets out of control, save book and plants

indicators.note: anything out of control runs wild, so the letters scatter into a new order
save can mean except, so a letter is left out

blocks.note: taken as written
B is the abbreviation for book

explanation.surface: As a fire spreads, a gardener rescues a book and some shrubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Save' reads as rescue, but it means except, removing B before the remaining letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Azaleas are flowering shrubs closely related to rhododendrons, so they are plants.

clue.text: Surely curious about one's first female pronoun

indicators.note: curious can mean odd or strange, so the letters take an odd new order
first picks out the opening letter only
about means around, so one piece surrounds another

blocks.note: taken as written
its opening letter
F is the abbreviation for female

explanation.surface: A grammarian is puzzled by which pronoun a woman uses.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged six letters wrap round the O, with F tacked on the end.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the second-person reflexive form, a word standing in for a noun.

clue.text: Model again on plonk ...

blocks.note: re means on or concerning
to plonk yourself down is to sit

explanation.surface: An artist's model poses once more, fuelled by cheap wine, and the dots lead on to the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: Plonk is British slang for cheap wine, but here it is the verb to plonk down. A model sits for an artist.
explanation.definitionFit: Artists' models sit for portraits, so to model again is to sit a second time.

clue.text: Mad London gangster loudly associating with two unknown characters

indicators.note: loudly points to speaking out, so the word is judged by its sound

blocks.note: the Kray twins were notorious 1960s East End London gangsters
in algebra x, y and z are unknowns

explanation.surface: A mad East End villain shouting while mixing with a couple of shady strangers.
explanation.walkthrough: Unknown characters are not strangers but algebra letters; the first syllable of the answer sounds like the gangster's surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Crazy and mad are everyday synonyms for wildly irrational or insane behaviour.

clue.text: ... is unable to bed captivating woman

indicators.note: to captivate is to hold captive, so one piece is trapped inside another

blocks.note: a cot is a small bed
Ann is a woman's name

explanation.surface: Continuing from the previous clue: a man who fails to seduce an alluring woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Captivating' looks like a description of the woman, but it tells the bed to hold her. The ellipsis just joins the two surfaces.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb form is a negative modal meaning lacks the ability, so it substitutes for is unable to.

clue.text: World's richest man cycling by front of market, getting fruit

indicators.note: cycling round means part of the word comes round from the front to the back
the front of a word is its opening letter
by means beside, so one piece sits next to another

blocks.note: Elon Musk, the tech billionaire
its opening letter

explanation.surface: A billionaire cycles past a market and picks up some fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: The billionaire's name rotates so the surname comes first, with M slotted between.
explanation.definitionFit: A muskmelon is a sweet orange-fleshed melon such as the cantaloupe, a common fruit.

clue.text: What might include Xmas card from flipping brother who hates Noel?

indicators.note: to flip something is to turn it over, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: Liam Gallagher of Oasis famously feuds with his brother Noel

explanation.surface: A Christmas card from a sibling who loathes Christmas.
explanation.walkthrough: Noel looks like Christmas, and 'flipping' like a mild British curse, but Noel is Noel Gallagher, whose brother is the Oasis singer.
explanation.definitionFit: Post delivered by the postal service could well contain a seasonal greetings card.

clue.text: Withdrawing, took home cheese

indicators.note: withdrawing is drawing back, so the letters go backwards

blocks.note: to make money is to take it home as pay

explanation.surface: Someone leaving a party takes home a piece of cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Took home' suggests carrying something away; it means earned, as in take-home pay.
explanation.definitionFit: Edam is a mild Dutch cheese sold in red-waxed rounds.

clue.text: Like park signs, except the odd ones

indicators.note: dropping the odd-numbered positions leaves only the even ones

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

explanation.surface: Someone likes the signs in a park, apart from a few strange ones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Odd ones' suggests weird signs; it means odd-numbered letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Akin means similar or related, so something akin to another is like it.

clue.text: Darts player is more tiddly

blocks.note: first meaning: the surname of the English teenager who won the PDC world darts title
second meaning: smaller, since tiddly is British slang for tiny

explanation.surface: A darts player getting tipsier as the pub match goes on.
explanation.walkthrough: Tiddly also means slightly drunk, which fits darts in a pub, but here it means tiny.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname of the English darts star doubles as a comparative of little, meaning smaller in size.

clue.text: Food cooked so eat it

indicators.note: cooking transforms ingredients, so the letters are worked into something new

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The meal is ready, so tuck in.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface fits the answer neatly: a toastie is a hot snack you would be told to eat.
explanation.definitionFit: A toastie is a British toasted sandwich, a kind of hot snack.
